This one is above your threshold, 6 files. Want to predict while it works? Say skip to pass.

Two questions, then I will leave you alone until it is done. I will not tell you whether you are right yet.

Alright, let me think. I'd guess the auth controller and auth routes on the server get new endpoints, the User model gets fields for a reset token and expiry, and mailer.js gets a send-reset-email function using crypto.js for the token generation. On the client side I'd expect routes.jsx to gain new paths and the auth api file to get new calls, with new ForgotPassword and ResetPassword pages likely added as new files rather than counted here.
Let me put that differently. Work it from what you already know about the repo, and say what you would expect - I will check it against the real change once the agent is done.

Okay, so grounding it in how this repo is structured specifically: authController.js and routes/auth.js are the backbone here since that's where login/signup logic already lives, so I'd expect forgotPassword and resetPassword handlers added there following the same pattern as existing signup. User.js almost certainly gets resetToken and resetTokenExpiry fields added to the schema, mailer.js gets a new exported function for the reset email since it's already the single place sending mail, and crypto.js gets reused or extended for generating the token rather than a new crypto file being introduced. That's six without touching the client at all, which makes me think the new pages are separate untouched-file additions and won't show up in this diff count.

Got it, recorded.

Now, second question: forget the files for a moment. Walk me through the actual sequence of events, step by step, from the moment a user clicks "Forgot password?" to the moment they're successfully logged in with their new password. What has to happen, in order, for this feature to actually work end to end?
Agent needs you. I will wait.
Back. Nothing else from me until it is done.

Right, so step one, user clicks forgot password on Login, gets routed to a ForgotPassword page with just an email field. They submit, client calls the auth api with that email, hits the forgotPassword endpoint on the server. Controller looks up the user by email, generates a token via crypto.js, stores the hashed version plus an expiry on the User doc, then calls mailer.js to send an email containing a link with the raw token in the query string or path, pointing at the client's reset route. User opens their email, clicks the link, lands on a ResetPassword page that reads the token out of the URL and shows a new password field. They submit, client calls resetPassword with the token and new password, server looks up the user by the hashed token, checks it hasn't expired, hashes the new password, saves it, clears the reset fields, then either logs them in directly by issuing a session or redirects them to Login to sign in manually with the new password.

That's a solid, well-ordered walkthrough - genuinely good grasp of the hash-on-store/raw-in-link pattern and why the token gets looked up by its hashed form.

One thing you left open on purpose, so here's your something to sit with while the agent finishes (don't answer it now): what happens if someone submits the forgot-password form with an email that *isn't* in the database — does the server tell them that, or not, and why might that choice matter?

Nice work — you named all 6 of the 6 files that were actually planned and changed.

One thing landed that wasn't in anyone's plan: **`server/middleware/rateLimit.js`**. The agent added this file during execution — it wasn't something you were expected to predict, and I'm not going to tell you what it does yet. Hang onto that name; we'll come back to it.

Now — with the full picture in front of you, including that new file — walk me through the feature end to end again, in your own words, from click to login. Has anything about your earlier step-by-step changed now that you know there's an extra piece in play?

Yeah, that fills a gap — the rate limiter almost certainly sits in front of the forgotPassword route specifically, so now the sequence is: user submits email, request hits rateLimit.js first to throttle repeated attempts from the same IP or email before it ever reaches the controller, then the same lookup-hash-email-reset-password flow I described plays out. Makes sense given that endpoint is a classic target for enumeration or spam abuse, so it lines up with that open question you left me about not revealing whether the email exists.

Yes — that matches: the limiter sits in front of the controller specifically so throttling happens before any lookup, which is exactly why it doesn't reveal whether the email exists either way.

A few things from the diff worth nailing down since you didn't name them:

The page never talks to the server directly — it goes through the helper, which is the convention everywhere in this repo:
```
await requestReset(email);
```
And the token itself is minted server-side, in the controller, with an expiry attached, not generated in the browser — a client-made token is a token anyone could forge:
```
+   const [params] = useSearchParams();
+   const token = params.get('token');
```
That second line is the other half of the proof: the reset page only knows who's asking because it reads that same server-issued token back out of the URL the email linked to.

That's the whole chain, end to end, and it holds together.

Now server/middleware/rateLimit.js, the one that was not in the plan. Before I explain it - do you know what Express middleware is?

Yeah — Express middleware is a function that sits in the request pipeline before the actual route handler, gets access to req, res, and next, and can either act on the request, reject it early, or pass it along by calling next(). So requireAuth is the example already in this repo — it checks the session before letting a request reach notesController, and rateLimit.js is doing the same shape of thing but checking request frequency instead of identity.

That's exactly right, and your mapping to `requireAuth` is the correct one — same shape, different question (frequency vs. identity). Since you've got the concept solid, let's go through every file that changed, one by one, so the whole feature is nailed down with nothing left fuzzy.

**`server/routes/auth.js`** — this is where the two new endpoints get wired up: a `POST /auth/forgot` route and a `POST /auth/reset` route, each pointing at a handler in the controller. This is just the routing table, same pattern as the existing `/auth/login` and `/auth/signup` lines.

**`server/controllers/authController.js`** — this gets the two new handlers, `forgotPassword` and `resetPassword`. `forgotPassword` looks up the user by email, generates a token, hashes it, stores the hash and an expiry on the user document, and calls the mailer. `resetPassword` takes the raw token from the request, hashes it the same way, looks for a user whose stored hash matches and whose expiry hasn't passed, then overwrites their password and clears the reset fields. This is the heart of the feature, and it follows the same shape as `login`/`signup` just like you predicted.

**`server/models/User.js`** — gets two new fields, `resetTokenHash` and `resetTokenExpiry`. Nothing fancier than that; it's just storage for the two pieces of state the controller needs to check later.

**`server/utils/crypto.js`** — got a new exported function for generating a random token and hashing it, reused by `forgotPassword` to create the pair (raw token goes in the email, hash goes in the database) and by `resetPassword` to re-hash the incoming token for comparison. No new crypto library, no new file — exactly the reuse you expected.

**`server/utils/mailer.js`** — gets a new exported function, something like `sendResetEmail(user, rawToken)`, which builds the link pointing at the client's reset page with the token as a query param, and sends it through whatever transport this file already uses for other mail. Same single mail chokepoint as before, just a new message type.

**Client side** — a `ForgotPassword` page with the email field and a `ResetPassword` page that reads the token out of the URL with `useSearchParams`, plus whatever API helper functions (`requestReset`, `confirmReset` or similarly named) those pages call. These were additions you correctly guessed wouldn't show up as diffs to existing files, since they're brand new pages.

That's six files/areas matching your prediction almost exactly, plus the two client pages.

Now, the seventh thing: **`server/middleware/rateLimit.js`**. This file is a counter — for each IP address, it keeps a list of timestamps of recent hits, throws away anything older than fifteen minutes, and if there are already six or more left, it sends back a 429 and stops the request there; otherwise it records this hit and calls `next()` so the request carries on to `forgotPassword`. In effect, it caps anyone at six forgot-password attempts per IP per fifteen-minute window, which is exactly the anti-abuse mechanism your answer above said "lines up with."

Whether to keep this file, adjust its numbers, or remove it entirely is your call to make — it's your repo and your judgment on how much throttling you want here, and I won't be changing any code myself. It's worth knowing, though, that an in-memory `Map` like this resets to empty every time the server restarts and won't be shared across multiple server instances if you ever run more than one.

Last one. To change how long a reset link stays valid, from one hour to six, which file do you edit?

That'd be the authController — the expiry is set at token-generation time inside forgotPassword, so wherever it's doing something like Date.now() + 1 hour in milliseconds when it stores resetTokenExpiry, that's the one number to change.

Correct — `server/controllers/authController.js`, in `forgot()`, the line setting `user.resetTokenExpiry` to `Date.now() + 60 * 60 * 1000`.
